steps.label: Do Now: Sound Lab Recap
steps.content:
Do Now: Sound Lab Recap

A quick recap of Sound Lab before today's file size work. Based on Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, June 2025, Question 1.

items.prompt: What is meant by the sample rate of a sound recording?
options: The number of samples (measurements) taken per second
The number of bits used to store each sample
The total number of samples in the whole recording
How loudly the recording is played back
items.explain: Sample rate counts how many measurements are taken each second - a separate setting from how each one is stored.

items.prompt: What is meant by the sample resolution of a sound recording?
options: The number of bits used to store each sample
The number of samples taken per second
The length of the recording in seconds
The number of separate audio channels
items.explain: Sample resolution is the number of bits per sample - more bits means each measurement is rounded less.

items.prompt: What is the term for one individual measurement of the sound wave taken during sampling?
items.explain: Each single measurement is a sample. Sound Lab used the same word for one point on the reconstruction line.

items.prompt: A recording's sample resolution is increased. What happens to its file size?
options: It increases, because more bits are stored for every sample
It decreases, because each sample takes less space
It stays the same - only the sample rate changes file size
It only changes if the recording is also made longer
items.explain: More bits per sample means more data for every measurement, so the whole file gets bigger.

steps.label: Bits, Bytes and Everything Above
steps.content:
Bits, Bytes and Everything Above

Every calculation so far this topic has ended in a number of bits - characters × bits per character, width × height × colour depth, sample rate × sample resolution. Turning that bit total into a file size uses one ladder of units, each one 1024 times bigger than the one below it.

  • 1 nibble = 4 bits (half a byte)
  • 1 byte = 8 bits = 2 nibbles
  • 1 kilobyte (KB / kibibyte, KiB) = 1024 bytes
  • 1 megabyte (MB / mebibyte, MiB) = 1024 KB
  • 1 gigabyte (GB / gibibyte, GiB) = 1024 MB

Cambridge exam papers use the exact names KiB, MiB and GiB for this ×1024 ladder - the same multiplier this course has already used for every file size readout in Pixel Lab and Sound Lab.

steps.label: Exam Question: Bits to Kibibytes
steps.content:
Exam Question: Bits to Kibibytes

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, June 2024, Question 1 - working with data storage units, then applying the width x height x colour depth formula from Pixel Lab.

items.prompt: (a) Give the name of the data storage measurement equal to 8 bits.
items.explain: 8 bits = 1 byte. A nibble is 4 bits (half a byte).

items.prompt: (b) How many bits are there in a kibibyte (KiB)?
items.explain: 1 KiB = 1024 bytes, and each byte is 8 bits, so 1024 x 8 = 8192 bits.

items.prompt: (c) Give the name of the data storage measurement equal to 1024 gibibytes (GiB).
items.explain: The ladder goes byte, KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB - each x1024. 1024 GiB = 1 TiB.

items.prompt: (d) A 16-bit colour image has a resolution of 512 pixels wide by 512 pixels high. Calculate the file size in kibibytes (KiB).
items.explain: 512 x 512 x 16 = 4,194,304 bits. Divide by 8 for bytes (524,288), then by 1024 for KiB = 512 KiB.

steps.label: Exam Question: The Same Ladder Again
steps.content:
Exam Question: The Same Ladder Again

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, March 2026, Question 1 - the unit ladder and a full image file size calculation together.

items.explain: Each step of the ladder is x1024, so two steps (TiB to EiB, via PiB) is 1024 x 1024. The other three break the ladder.

items.prompt: (b) An image is 1024 pixels high x 1024 pixels wide with a colour depth of two bytes. Calculate the file size in MiB.
items.explain: 1024 x 1024 = 1,048,576 pixels, x 2 bytes = 2,097,152 bytes. Divide by 1024 twice (to KiB then MiB) = 2 MiB.

steps.label: From Bits/Sec to a Full File
steps.content:
From Bits/Sec to a Full File

Sound Lab worked out bits per second (sample rate × sample resolution). A full recording also has a length - multiply by the duration in seconds to get the whole file's size.

Total: 2 marks

steps.label: Plenary: File Size
steps.content:
Plenary: File Size

Answer from memory - no notes, no going back to the challenges.

items.explain: Every step of the data storage ladder is x1024, so 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.

items.prompt: How many bits are there in 1 byte?
items.explain: 1 byte = 8 bits. A nibble is 4 bits.

items.prompt: Why does a text file with more characters have a larger file size?
options: Each character is stored using a fixed number of bits, so more characters means more bits
More characters need a higher colour depth
The file adds one byte of metadata per character
Longer files are always compressed less
items.explain: File size = number of characters x bits per character, so the total grows with the character count.

items.prompt: Calculate the file size, in bytes, of a 20-character message stored using 16-bit Unicode.

y10_1_2_l4_examunits.feedback: 1 byte is 2 nibbles - multiply the byte count by 2.
Divide by 1024 to move up one step of the ladder.
Multiply by 1024 to move down one step of the ladder.
Every step of the ladder is the same ×1024 jump, all the way up to exbibytes.

Take your answer to part (a) and divide by 8.

y10_1_2_l4_practice.feedback: Multiply the character count by the bits used for each character.
